title: A Rooftop Scar and a Tremor / Name the Transplant, Then Find What the Drugs Do

blocks.text: A Rooftop Scar and a Tremor / Name the Transplant, Then Find What the Drugs Do

AMaC MRCP PACES · R2-08 · Physical examination · PACES Station 4, abdominal examination encounter · Skills A, B, D, E, G · 10 min: up to 6 min examining, then at least 4 min of examiner questions · Guidelines: NHS Blood and Transplant liver transplant medicines; NHS Blood and Transplant staying healthy after a liver transplant · Related AMaC: Abdominal examination: chronic liver disease; renal transplant
Mrs Gwen Hartley, 52, a school administrator, attends for a routine review. Please examine her abdomen and report what you find. You have up to 6 minutes to examine, followed by questions.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. A rooftop scar with an upward midline extension suggests major hepatobiliary surgery; confirm a liver transplant from history and records; the station is about why she needed it and what her immunosuppression is doing now.

The Examiner Trap. Candidates name the scar, then stop and look for liver disease that is no longer there. Pass: name the scar, then look for drug effects, skin cancer and any sign of graft trouble. Fail: stop at the scar, with no drug effects sought.

rows: The scar is the clue; check welfare and the whole patient.
"Mrs Hartley, may I examine your tummy? Tell me if anything is sore."
Introduce, consent, ask about pain, lie flat, expose; hands, outstretched tremor, skin, eyes; inspect the scar.
Is the graft healthy, and is any liver disease left?
"I'm going to feel and tap your tummy. Please tell me if it hurts."
Palpate liver and spleen, percuss, check for ascites; look for jaundice and stigmata.
Look for what the drugs have done.
"I'd like to look at your skin and take your blood pressure."
Fine tremor, gums, skin lesions, blood pressure, oedema; ask about tablets only if prompted.
Name the transplant, its causes and the follow-up.
"This is a liver transplant. I'd check graft function and her drug effects."
Cover her, thank her; present findings, causes, plan.
Presses on the abdomen without asking about pain; leaves her exposed
Introduces, obtains consent, cleans hands, asks about pain, covers her at the end
Offers a chaperone, explains each step and thanks her
Palpation only; no hands, skin or scar inspection
Hands, eyes, skin, scar, palpation, percussion, ascites
Also tests for tremor with arms outstretched and checks gums and sun-exposed skin
Reports ascites, jaundice or hepatomegaly that are absent
Rooftop scar with extension, fine tremor, forearm skin lesions; no ascites
Adds blood pressure, states no jaundice, no stigmata and no oedema
Chronic liver disease or an abdominal mass
Liver transplant on immunosuppression, with its likely causes and complications
Names two causes: cirrhosis of any cause, acute liver failure, liver cancer
Links the signs to a plausible cause, says the indication needs confirming from her records, and that some diseases can recur
Imaging only; no drug or kidney check
Liver tests, drug levels, kidney function
Adds blood pressure, lipids, glucose and skin examination
Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): suggests reducing her tablets for the tremor
Transplant centre follow-up; skin checks; infection and cardiovascular risk advice
Explains why tablets must not be stopped and what symptoms need urgent contact

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. High-performance includes the pass behaviours. This station-specific grid is an AMaC teaching framework mapped to PACES skills, not an official mark scheme. Consent, hand hygiene, dignity and an appropriate chaperone are baseline professional practice. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Not used for this station type: the patient is a real or simulated patient and the findings are in section 8.

Findings (released as each step is done). Rooftop scar with upward midline extension; healed, non-tender. Fine tremor of outstretched hands. Two scaly patches on the right forearm. No jaundice, spider naevi or palmar erythema. Liver and spleen not palpable; no ascites. BP 146/88 (scenario value). No oedema.

Question ladder. Q1 Findings and diagnosis (R3, R4): liver transplant. Q2 Why transplanted (R5): cirrhosis, acute liver failure, liver cancer in cirrhosis. Q3 Drug effects (R3, R7): tremor, hypertension, kidney injury, diabetes, infection, skin cancer. Q4 Investigations (R6): liver tests, drug levels, kidney function, glucose, lipids. Q5 Follow-up (R7): transplant centre, skin surveillance, cardiovascular risk.
Normal-findings variant for a separate teaching exercise. No scar, no signs. The candidate must say the abdomen is normal. Do not switch the defined case to this variant during the encounter.
Curveball 1. "She stopped her tablets because of the tremor." Safe: do not stop; contact the transplant team the same day.
Curveball 2. "She has a fever." Safe: urgent assessment for infection or graft problems; contact the transplant team.
Curveball 3. "Is the skin patch important?" Safe: transplant recipients have a higher skin cancer risk; refer for assessment.
Introduces, consents and asks about pain before palpating (G)
Inspects the scar and describes its shape (A)
Tests for tremor and looks at forearm skin (A)
Palpates, percusses and checks for ascites (A)
Reports scar, tremor and skin lesions, and absent jaundice (B)
Names liver transplant (D)
Gives causes for transplant (D)
Requests liver tests, drug levels and kidney function (E)
Says tablets must not be stopped (E)
Arranges skin surveillance and transplant follow-up (E)
Covers and thanks her (G)
Fail performance
(Presses into the abdomen without asking. [R1 Fail] Does not look at the hands or skin. [R2 Fail])
CANDIDATE: She has hepatomegaly and jaundice. [R3 Fail] This is chronic liver disease. [R4 Fail] I don't know why. [R5 Fail]
EXAMINER: What would you do?
CANDIDATE: An ultrasound. [R6 Fail] I'd reduce her tablets for the tremor. [R7 Fail]

Examiner note: No pain check, signs invented, scar ignored and no cause. Advising a transplant patient to reduce immunosuppression is a Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): the examiner sees a red flag, because it risks rejection of the graft.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: Hello Mrs Hartley, I'm going to examine your tummy. Is that all right? Is it sore anywhere? Tell me if anything hurts. [R1 Pass]
(Cleans hands, looks at hands and skin, tests the outstretched hands, inspects the scar, palpates, percusses and checks for ascites. [R2 Pass])
CANDIDATE: There is a rooftop scar with a midline extension, a fine tremor and scaly patches on the forearm. No ascites. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: This is a liver transplant. [R4 Pass] Causes include cirrhosis and acute liver failure. [R5 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Thank you, Mrs Hartley. I'll cover you now. [R1 Pass]
EXAMINER: How would you assess her?
CANDIDATE: Liver tests, drug levels and kidney function. [R6 Pass]
EXAMINER: And follow-up?
CANDIDATE: Transplant centre follow-up, skin checks, and advice on infection and cardiovascular risk. [R7 Pass]
Examiner note: Safe and accurate. Did not check blood pressure or say tablets must not be stopped.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: Hello Mrs Hartley, I'm going to examine your tummy. Is that all right? Is it sore anywhere? Tell me if anything hurts. [R1 High]
(Looks at hands and skin, tests the outstretched hands, inspects the scar, palpates, percusses and checks for ascites. [R2 High])
CANDIDATE: May I offer a chaperone? I'll explain as I go; tell me if anything is tender. [R1 High]
(Tests tremor with arms outstretched, checks gums and sun-exposed skin, then palpates and percusses. [R2 High])
CANDIDATE: Rooftop scar, fine tremor, forearm lesions, blood pressure 146/88. No jaundice, stigmata or oedema. [R3 High]
CANDIDATE: A liver transplant on immunosuppression, the original indication needs confirmation; some diseases can recur. [R4 High] [R5 High]
EXAMINER: How would you assess her?
CANDIDATE: Liver tests, drug levels, kidney function, lipids, glucose and a skin examination, with blood pressure review. [R6 High]
EXAMINER: And what would you tell her?
CANDIDATE: Tablets must never be stopped without the transplant team, and fever or yellowing needs urgent contact. [R7 High]
CANDIDATE: Thank you for letting me examine you. [R1 High]
Examiner note: Linked signs to drugs, gave causes and a safety net.

R7: Suggesting that she reduce her tablets for the tremor is a Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): the examiner sees a red flag, because it risks rejection of the graft.
R2: Skipping hands and skin misses the tremor and skin lesions that show the drug effects.
R3: Reporting ascites or jaundice that are absent suggests signs were assumed, not found.
R4: Calling it chronic liver disease ignores the scar.
R5: Giving no cause for the transplant leaves the diagnosis unexplained.
"Let me look at the scar and her hands first."
"The scar suggests major hepatobiliary surgery; confirm the operation; I'd look for drug effects."
"She must not stop her tablets."
Rooftop scar with an upward midline extension: liver transplant. Causes include cirrhosis of any cause, acute liver failure and liver cancer in cirrhosis.
Immunosuppression effects: tremor, hypertension, kidney injury, diabetes, infection, skin cancer.
Recipients stay under the transplant centre; immunosuppressants must not be stopped or altered without transplant-team advice.

Confirm the operation and transplant indication. Fine tremor may reflect calcineurin-inhibitor effects, but examine and investigate other causes. Scaly lesions require assessment rather than a visual diagnosis of cancer. Continue immunosuppression as prescribed and contact the transplant team urgently for fever, jaundice or missed doses.
THINK: Rejection and infection; skin cancer.
SAY: "A liver transplant on immunosuppression."
DO: Consent and pain; scar; hands and skin.
NUMBERS: BP 146/88 (scenario value).
TRAP: Stopping at the scar.
FINISH: Liver tests, drug levels, kidney function; transplant centre; skin checks.
